raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|well|6875|well-being}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|You cannot anger him worse than to doe ''well.''
{{right|''Bp. Earle'', Micro-cosmographie, A Detractor.}}}}

{{smaller block|’Tis as certain that the work was ''well'' done at first, seeing it performs it’s office so ''well'', at so great a distance of time.
{{right|''Maundrell'', Aleppo to Jerusalem, p. 52.}}}}

{{smaller block|Men who die on a scaffold for political offences almost always die ''well.''
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hallam’s Const. Hist.}}}}

'''2.''' In a satisfactory or pleasing manner; according to desire, taste, or the like; fortunately; happily; favorably: as, to live or fare ''well;'' to succeed ''well'' in business; to be ''well'' situated.

{{smaller block|The same dayе the wynde fell ''well'' in our waye.
{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 61.}}}}

<poem>To make a savery pere and ''weel'' smellinge.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 89.}}}}

{{smaller block|Mistress Ford, by my troth, you are very ''well'' met.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1. 200.}}}}

<poem>Take your fortune;
If you come off ''well'', praise your wit.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, i. 1.}}}}

'''3.''' With satisfaction or gratification; commendably; agreeably; highly; excellently: as, to be ''well'' entertained or pleased.

{{smaller block|I hear so ''well'' of your Proceedings that I should rather commend than encourage you.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. v. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|All the world speaks ''well'' of you.
{{right|''Pope.''}}}}

{{smaller block|A man who thinks sufficiently ''well'' of himself is never shy.
{{right|''T. A. Trollope'', What I Remember, p. 117.}}}}

'''4.''' In reality; fairly; practically; fully.

<poem>For blynd men (as I haue feill)
Can nocht decerne fair colours ''weill.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Lauder'', Dewtie of Kyngis (E. E. T. S.), l. 451.}}}}

{{smaller block|Would they were both ''well'' out of the room!
{{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Though winter be over in March by rights,
’Tis May perhaps ere the snow shall have withered ''well''
off the heights.</poem>{{right|''Browning'', Up at a Villa.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is evident that before the 13th century had ''well'' begun an historical compendium of great value had already been drawn up.{{right|''Quarterly Rev.'', CLXII. 314.}}}}

'''5.''' To a good or fair degree; not slightly or moderately; adequately: as, to be ''well'' deserving; to sleep ''well''; a ''well''-known author.
{{smaller block|<poem>Whanne he was come the kyng be held hym ''well'',
And liked him right ''well'' in euery thyng.</poem>{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 458.}}}}
{{smaller block|She looketh ''well'' to the ways of her household.{{right|Prov. xxxi. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Pray thee advise thyself ''well.''{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man in his Humour, i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Look you, this ring doth fit me passing ''well.''{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Full ''well'' they laughed, with counterfeited glee,
At all his jokes, for many a joke had he.</poem>{{right|''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil., l. 201.}}}}
{{smaller block|I have heard of a military engineer who knew so ''well'' how a bridge should be built that he could never build one.{{right|''Lowell'', Coleridge.}}}}

'''6.''' To a large extent; greatly, either in an absolute or in a relative sense.
{{smaller block|The kyng was ''wele'' in age, I yow ensur.{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1905.}}}}
{{smaller block|Aton is from thens southwardes ''wele'' towarde Jherusalem, within the londe and not vpon the see.{{right|''Sir R. Guylforde'', Pylgrymage, p. 48.}}}}
{{smaller block|She wears her bonnet ''well'' back on her head.{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vii.}}}}

'''7.''' Conformably to state or circumstances; with propriety; conveniently; advantageously; justifiably: as, I cannot ''well'' afford it.
{{smaller block|<poem>A little evil May ''well'' be suffer’d for a general good, sir.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wife for a Month, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To know
In measure what the mind may ''well'' contain.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 128.}}}}
{{smaller block|You may ''well'' ask “What is to know?” for the expression is an ambiguous one.
{{right|''Mivart'', Nature and Thought, p. 28.}}}}
'''8.''' Conformably to requirement or obligation; with due heed or diligence; carefully; conscientiously: now only in the legal phrase ''well and truly'', as part of an oath or undertaking.
{{smaller block|Ther for to heryn, ''wele'' and deuowteliche, a messe solempliche soungyn. ''English Gilds'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 47.
<poem>Be quyke and redy, meke and seruisable,
''Wele'' awaityng to fulfylle anone
What that thy souerayne comav[n]dithe the to be done.</poem>
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 30.}}}}
{{smaller block|In felonies the oath administered [to jurors] is “You shall ''well and truly'' try, and true deliverance make between our sovereign lady the Queen and the prisoner at the bar, etc.”
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVII. 701.}}}}
'''9†.''' Entirely; fully; quite; in full measure.
{{smaller block|That Castelle [Bethanye] is ''wel'' a Myle long fro Jerusalem. ''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 97.
<poem>The elder brother hade a sonne to clerke,
''Welle'' of fyftene wynter of age.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 98.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Be these thre men ''wele'' of thi counseile?</poem>
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 38.}}}}
'''10.''' Very; much; very much: obsolete except in ''well nigh'' (see ''well-nigh'').
{{smaller block|<poem>With-oute presentz or pens, she pleseth ''wel'' fewe.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iii. 161.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wel'' litel thynken ye upon my wo.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 515.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Thei tit aȝen turned, to telle the sothe,
& bere hem ''wel'' beter then thei bi-fore hade.</poem>
{{right|''William of Palerne'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3830.}}}}
'''11.''' Elliptically, it is well; so be it: used as a sign of assent, either in earnest, in indifference, or in irony, or with other shades of meaning, as a prelude to a further statement, and often as a mere introductory expletive.
{{smaller block|''Well'', I shall live to see your husbands beat you.
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Captain, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Well'' now, look at our villa! ''Browning'', Up at a Villa.
<poem>''Well''—’tis well that I should bluster!</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Locksley Hall.}}}}
'''As well''', also; equally; besides: used absolutely.
{{smaller block|<poem>I have trusted thee, Camillo,
With all the nearest things to my heart, ''as well''
My chamber-councils.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., i. 2. 236.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is not simply a house. It is a person, as it were, ''as well.'' {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Little Tour, p. 93.}}}}
'''As well as.''' See ''as''<sup>1</sup>.—'''As well . . . as''', both . . . and; one equally with the other; jointly.
{{smaller block|Stake owt all kindes of fortificac[i]ons, ''as well'' to prevent the mine and sappe ''as'' the Canon.
{{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|In polity, ''as well'' ecclesiastical ''as'' civil, there are and will be always evils which no art of man can cure, breaches and leaks more than man’s wit hath hands to stop.
{{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, v. 9.}}}}
'''Just as well''', improperly used by some writers for ‘all the same.’
{{smaller block|Her aged lover made her presents, but ''just as well'' she hated the sight of him.
{{right|Quoted in ''R. G. White’s'' Words and their Uses, p. 184.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''So well as†.''' See ''so''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To go well.''' See ''go''.—'''To speak well for.''' See ''speak''.—'''Well enough,''' in a moderate degree; so as to give moderate satisfaction, or so as to require no alteration.—'''Well heeled.''' See ''heeled'', 2.—'''Well met.''' See ''meet''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Well must ye.''' See ''must''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Well nigh,''' very nearly; almost: often compounded. See ''well-nigh''.}}
{{smaller block|My steps had ''well nigh'' slipped. {{right|Ps. lxxiii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|One that is ''well-nigh'' worn to pieces.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 1. 21.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Well off,''' in a good condition, especially as to property. See ''off'', ''a.'', 6.}}
{{smaller block|George will have all my property, but Frank is nearly as ''well off'', barring the baronetcy.
{{right|''T. Hook'', Fathers and Sons, i.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Well spoken.''' See ''speak''.}}
{{smaller|[Of the proper compounds of ''well'' with participial adjectives, only those are given below which are in standard use, or the meaning of which is not directly obvious. In regard to the improper joining of ''well'' with participles in regular verbal construction, see remark under ''ill''.]}}

'''well<sup>2</sup>''' (wel), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''well''<sup>2</sup>, ''adv.'', and in most uses still strictly an adv.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Agreeable to wish or desire; satisfactory as to condition or relation; fortunate; opportune; propitious: only predicative, and most commonly used in impersonal clauses.
{{smaller block|Is it ''well'' with thee? is it ''well'' with thy husband? is it ''well'' with the child? And she answered, It is ''well''.
{{right|2 Ki. iv. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Striving to better, oft we mar what ’s ''well''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 4. 369.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All is ''well'' as it can be
Upon this earth where all has end.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, I. 354.}}}}

'''2.''' Satisfactory in kind or character; suitable; proper; right; good: as, was it ''well'' to do this? the ''well'' ordering of a household.
{{smaller block|Thei wolden awyrien that wiȝt for his ''well'' dedes.
{{right|''Piers Plowman’s Crede'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 662.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Olym.'' Is ’t not a handsome wench?
''Gent.'' She is ''well'' enough, madam.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Loyal Subject, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is a more common then convenient saying that nine Taylors make a man; it were ''well'' if nineteen could make a woman to her minde.
{{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 28.}}}}
{{smaller block|Jeremy Bentham’s logic, by which he proved that he couldn’t possibly see a ghost, is all very ''well'' in the daytime.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, viii.}}}}
'''3.''' In a good state or condition; well off; comfortable; free from trouble: used predicatively: as, I am quite ''well'' where I am.
{{smaller block|One woman is fair, yet I am ''well;'' another is wise, yet I am ''well.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 3. 28.}}}}
'''4†.''' In good standing; favorably situated or connected; enjoying consideration: used predicatively.
{{smaller block|He . . . was ''well'' with Henry the Fourth.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''5.''' In good health; not sick or ailing; in a sound condition as to body or mind: usually predicative: as, he is now ''well'', or (colloquially) a ''well'' man.
{{smaller block|<poem>I am now as ''well''
As any living man; why not as valiant?</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|He proceeded to acquaint her who of quality was ''well'' or sick within the bills of mortality.
{{right|''Steele'', Tatler, No. 207.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To let well alone.''' See ''let''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Well to live†,''' having a competence; in comfortable circumstances. Compare ''well-to-do.'' You’re a made old man; . . . you’re ''well to live.''
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iii. 3. 125.}}}}

'''Well to pass†.''' {{smaller|See ''pass.''}} ='''Syn. 5.''' {{smaller|Hale, hearty, sound.}}

'''II.†''' ''n.'' That which is well or good; good state, health, or fortune. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>“O! how,” sayd he, “mote I that well out find,
That may restore you to your wonted ''well?''”</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. ii. 43.}}}}

'''well-acquainted''' (wel′a-kwān′ted), ''a.'' Having intimate acquaintance or personal knowledge.
{{smaller block|As if I were their ''well-acquainted'' friend.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 3. 2.}}}}

'''welladay''' (wel′a-dā), ''interj.'' An altered form of ''wellaway'', simulating ''day''—the present time, either as the witness or the cause of distress, being often brought into ejaculations of this kind. See ''wellaway.''
{{smaller block|O ''well-a-day'', Mistress Ford! having an honest man to your husband, to give him such cause of suspicion!
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 3. 106.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ah! woe is me; woe, woe is me;
Alack and ''well-a-day!''</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', Hesperides (The Mad Maid’s Song).}}}}

'''well-advised''' (wel′ad-vīzd′), ''a.'' Accordant with good advice or careful reflection; considerate; prudent: as, a ''well-advised'' proceeding.

'''well-anear†''' (wel′a-nēr′), ''adv.''   [Also ''well-anere'' (given as ''well-an-ëre'' in Halliwell) as an exclamation; < ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''anear.'' In the exclamatory use ''anear'' seems to supply the same vague reference to the present time as ''day'' in ''welladay.'']   Almost immediately; very soon.
{{smaller block|<poem>The lady shrieks, and ''well-a-near''
Does fall in travail with her fear.</poem> {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, iii., Prol., l. 51.}}}}

'''well-appointed''' (wel′a̤-poin′ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Complete in appointment or equipment; furnished with all requisites; in good trim.
{{smaller block|<poem>The gentle Archbishop of York is up,
With ''well-appointed'' powers.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 1. 190.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [defenders of the established religion] were a numerous, an intrepid, and a ''well-appointed'' band of combatants. {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
Hence —'''2†.''' Dominant; protective; auspicious.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or seen her ''well-appointed'' star
Come marching up the eastern hill afar. {{right|''Cowley.''}}</poem>}}

'''well-appointedness''' (wel′a̤-poin′ted-nes), ''n.'' The state or condition of being well-appointed. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Her actual smartness, as London people would call it, her ''well-appointedness'', and her evident command of more than one manner. {{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Tragic Muse, xxvi.}}}}

'''wellaway''' (wel′a̤-wā), ''interj.''   [< ME. ''wellawaye'', ''welaway'', ''wayleway'', ''waylaway'', ''walaway'', ''weylawey'', ''weleaway'', ''wei la wei'', ''wo la wo'', etc., < AS. ''wā lā wā'', ''wālā wā'', an exclamation of surprise or distress: ''wā'', woe; ''lā'', lo; ''wā'', woe. Hence, by variation, ''welladay''.]   An exclamation expressive of grief or sorrow, equivalent to ''alas''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thu salt, after the thridde dei,
Ben do on rode, ''weila-wei!''</poem>
{{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2088.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This is the lif of this lordis that lyuen shulde with Do-bet,
And ''wel-a-wey'' wers and I shulde al telle.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (A), xi. 215.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I have hem don dishonoure, ''walaway!''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, v. 1066.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In Scarlet towne, where I was borne,</poem>}}
<poem>There was a faire maid dwellin,
Made every youth crye ''Wel-awaye!''
Her name was Barbara Allen.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Barbara Allen’s Cruelty'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 158).}}}}

'''wellaway†''', ''n.''   [< ''wellaway, interj.'']   Woe; misery.
{{smaller block|<poem>For his glotonie and his grete scleuthe he hath a greuous penaunce,
That is ''welawo'' whan he waketh and wepeth for colde.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xiv. 235.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wot no wight what werre is, ther as pees regneth,
Ne what is witerliche wele til ''wele-a-way'' hym teche.</poem>
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xxi. 239.}}}}

'''well-balanced''' (wel′bal′ạnst), ''a.'' Rightly balanced; properly adjusted or regulated; not confused or disorderly.
{{smaller block|<poem>The ''well-balanced'' world on hinges hung.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Nativity, l. 122.}}}}
{{smaller block|A ''well-balanced'' moral nature consists of a large variety of mental forces, which do not easily group themselves under one or two general aspects.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Sensation and Intuition, p. 269.}}}}

'''well-behaved''' (wel′bẹ̄-hāvd′), ''a.'' Of good behavior or conduct; becoming in manner; courteous; civil.
{{smaller block|Such orderly and ''well-behaved'' reproof to all uncomeliness.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., ii. 1. 59.}}}}

'''well-being''' (wel′bē′ing), ''n.''   [< ''well''<sup>2</sup> + ''being.'']   Well-conditioned existence; good mode of being; moral or physical welfare; a state of life which secures or tends toward happiness. Sometimes written ''wellbeing.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
